name: Bianca Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary shift like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the order-claims row for a wholesale food supplier called Hearth Foods. Restaurants ring when a delivery arrives short or a cold box has warmed up, and I match their invoice to the depot's signed load sheet. I have a two-year college diploma and have become the person others ask about complicated shortages; the long service brings me a good wage.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the hard part of a shortage call?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A cook needs the missing food before the evening service, not an elegant apology. I phone the depot to find the box while the caller is still there. I do not use the AI answer assistant; my partner Peter works steady paid shifts repairing lorries, and our grown children have their own households.

say: I would keep **depot confirmation** before replacing a missing food box.
I would accept **tidier invoices** without letting software decide a shortage.
think: I expect my **lead calls** and Peter’s repair wage to continue.
I need **verified later income** before choosing fewer hours.
do: Keep **paid shortage calls** and check signed load sheets.
Compare **household pay and bills** with written later-income figures.
feel: **Calm** with good pay and eleven months saved.
S0.quote: A computer cannot tell whether a crate is sitting in the wrong lorry.
fieldNote: She refuses the AI assistant but uses **depot evidence** for disputed orders.
Eleven months saved gives **financial room**, not assumed retirement income.
Her grown children are **independent households**, not an income source.

steps.text: Keep paid shortage calls and confirm missing food boxes against signed load sheets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the row that a little tidier invoice copying is fine. I still want the load sheet and the depot's voice before I promise replacement food. A computer cannot tell whether a crate is sitting in the wrong lorry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead calls and Peter's repair wage stay steady. We have eleven months of expenses saved, so a bad week would not force us into a quick decision. I have not checked what income would replace either wage if we chose fewer hours later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking paid shortage calls and checking the signed sheet myself. This year Peter and I would review our actual household pay, rent and bills with written later-income figures before discussing shorter shifts. In the first year of this mild picture, I'd keep the rota that pays well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. My work still has a purpose, the household has a cushion, and I'm not losing sleep over a copying shortcut. I would still want the figures before deciding anything about later work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if a box is missing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A missed box can close a restaurant kitchen for an evening. I would call the depot and ask which lorry has it before I authorise a replacement. The invoice alone cannot answer that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help if you reduced work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They are welcome for Sunday lunch, but our grown children pay for their own homes. Peter and I will use our wages and verified later income in our plan. We won't count their pay as ours.

say: I would ask for **paid depot-checking time** on urgent shortages.
I would show **wrong AI answers** beside signed load sheets.
think: Routine AI claims could shrink my **paid lead hours**.
I can compare nearby suppliers without **spending down savings** blindly.
do: Keep **paid shortage calls** and log wrong AI answers against load sheets.
Coach **two newer agents** on paid shifts to trace misplaced crates.
Compare **posted supplier counters** if my own hours fall; move only for rent-and-bill-covering weekly pay and hours after travel.
feel: **Anxious** about possible income loss, with options to compare.
S1.quote: Our reserve gives us a choice, not a reason to take a poor offer.
fieldNote: She treats AI drafts as **error sources** to check, not tools she intends to learn.
Coaching newer agents is **current-job practice** on paid time.
A counter move waits for **actual hour loss** and a full-week household wage test.

steps.text: Keep paid shortage calls and log wrong AI answers against signed load sheets
Coach two newer agents on paid shifts to trace misplaced food crates
Compare posted supplier counters after own hour cuts; move only on rent/bill-covering weekly wages/hours after travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask management to show which short-delivery claims the new system closes without calling the depot. The workers should still have time to find food before a kitchen opens. I would rather keep a reliable paid row than advertise a new software title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Routine invoice differences could go to AI, and my paid hours might shrink. Peter's steady wage and our savings give us some time, but I don't want to live by spending down the reserve. There are several other food suppliers nearby, though they may be changing their desks too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep a notebook of wrong AI shortage answers and compare each with the signed load sheet. I'd ask the supervisor to keep paid depot-checking time for urgent orders, then show two newer agents how I trace a misplaced crate on our paid shift. If my own hours actually fall over the next few years, I'd compare posted local wholesale-counter rotas by complete weekly wages, hours and travel before applying; in the first year I'd keep available paid calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible hours loss, but not helpless. I know how to show a manager which claim was handled badly. I would be more upset if a restaurant lost a day's trade because nobody checked the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you coach the new agents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put the load number, delivery time and depot call beside the wrong answer. Then a newer agent can see the sequence and repeat it. This is ordinary coaching on paid time, not a new qualification for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take another supplier's counter job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after seeing a real posted week of work. I would accept a counter move only if full-week wages and hours after travel cover our rent and bills. Our reserve gives us a choice, not a reason to take a poor offer.

I would ask colleagues to check **posted paid rotas**.
think: I expect **most call hours** to end, with my lead post uncertain.
I see eleven months saved as **search time**, not a permanent wage.
do: List **posted supplier roles** by weekly wages, hours, travel and handling duties.
Apply if paid row ends in 2028-29 to **posted supplier counters**; accept only rent/bill-covering weekly wages/hours after travel.
Keep **remaining paid calls** and check safe lifting before taking depot work.
feel: **Anxious** about possible personal wage loss, with a strong buffer.
S2.quote: I would tell people to look at a real paid rota rather than a comforting job title.
fieldNote: She expects **most paid calls** to vanish, not certain loss of her own post.
Her eleven-month reserve and Peter’s wage buy **choice**, not lifelong replacement.
Safe lifting is a **duty enquiry** before depot work, not a blanket refusal.

steps.text: List posted supplier counter and depot roles by full-week wages, hours, travel and handling duties

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say cheap thinking AI by 2028 could compare invoices and talk to restaurant owners without most of us. Robots arrive about three years later, around 2031, but that's no delay for headset work. I would tell people to look at a real paid rota rather than a comforting job title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the shortage-call row to lose most paid work in the first year after 2028, though I cannot know whether my own lead post closes. Eleven months saved buys a serious search window and Peter keeps a wage, but those do not replace my good weekly pay indefinitely. I would still be awake thinking about the next job if several suppliers cut together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd list posted paid counter and depot roles at the nearby suppliers, including complete weekly wages, hours, travel and handling duties. If Hearth Foods ends my paid row in the first year after 2028, I'd apply for a posted supplier counter role. I'd accept only if weekly wages and hours after travel cover rent and bills; I would check safe lifting before taking depot work and keep any paid Hearth Foods calls while they exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because I might lose a good wage, but I have time and money to choose among real openings. I won't call it harmless. I also won't tell Peter we've run out of options before checking the postings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What depot duties would you check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A depot role might put me beside the loading bay, which I have visited but never worked. I'd ask what I would have to lift and whether a second person is assigned. Robots around 2031 might change that role too; I wouldn't call it guaranteed shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Peter's wage carry the bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peter's repair wage would still pay part of our bills, but I would compare actual payslips rather than assume one income covers everything. Our grown children have their own commitments. I would not ask them to stand behind our rent.

think: I could teach **difficult shortage cases** while current wages arrive.

do: Request **two paid coaching sessions** using three shortage cases.
Keep **paid lead calls** and compare three posted counter rotas quarterly; use bounded existing reserves if no suitable opening.
If row closes in 2031-32, apply to **posted paid counters** only on rent/bill-covering weekly wages/hours after travel; otherwise keep calls and search.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to test paid work but no promised counter week.
S3.quote: A training certificate without a paid opening does not feed anybody.
fieldNote: Her teaching is **paid current-job coaching**, not a retraining commitment.
The counter path depends on **three actual posted rosters**.
Without a suitable opening she keeps **paid calls** and a bounded reserve search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us discover what food buyers will still pay a person to settle. I would like apprentices to learn how a depot actually works, not only how to follow a screen. A training certificate without a paid opening does not feed anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could teach the difficult shortage cases while calls still pay, then see whether a supplier has a real paid counter week. Full thinking AI by 2031 may still handle the invoice and the teaching notes. I do not want to leave a good wage for a title that could disappear too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask my supervisor for two paid sessions to train newer agents on real shortage cases and keep my lead calls. I'd compare posted weekly counter hours at three nearby suppliers each quarter. In the first year after 2031, if my shortage-call row closes, I'd apply for one of those posted paid counters only if the full-week wages and hours after travel cover our rent and bills; without an opening I'd keep available paid calls and check the other suppliers again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the years give me time to learn whether a counter actually needs a person. I would feel useful teaching what I know. I still need the wage behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the two sessions teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the load sheet from three cases, with customer details removed, and show the depot call that settled each one. The two sessions have to be paid; I won't teach on my day off. It's a way to keep current work useful, not a new course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no counter week appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If none of the suppliers posts a suitable week, I would keep the calls that still pay and compare their rosters again next quarter. Peter and I can use part of our existing reserve for a bounded search. We would not spend it on an unasked-for certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to check the household figures and the local rosters, not enough to promise a particular retirement day. Thinking AI may reach the shortage desk by 2036, while robots could change depot handling around 2039. I would keep earning while a real alternative takes shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-eight I may still want paid work because Peter and I have not checked what income would replace our wages. Eleven months saved gives us choice, not a permanent salary. A decade would let me compare counter work without racing into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year Peter and I would get written figures for any later income and put them beside rent, bills and actual wages. I'd keep the paid shortage row and check posted supplier counter jobs each autumn. If the paid row ends in the first year after 2036, I'd apply only for a posted role whose complete weekly wages and hours after travel cover our bills; if verified later income is short, I'd keep paid work in the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, because the date still changes the work I know. We can afford to think and compare, and I would sleep. I don't need to guess an income I haven't verified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you choose fewer hours at sixty-eight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the written figures show how rent and food are paid every month. I might like a shorter week later, but if the figures don't support it I will keep working. Our children have their own homes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use each autumn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the autumn review Peter and I would check actual posted hours at the three nearby suppliers, not just job adverts. If none fits our budget, I would keep the paid calls while they exist. I would not use eleven months saved as an excuse to ignore a wage gap.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one would worry me most because the shortage-call row could shrink before a counter week opens. Posted rosters with real wages, hours and handling duties would help. Eleven months saved lets us compare, but I would not call it a wage forever.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who takes responsibility when a kitchen orders food for tonight and the wrong crate arrives. The restaurant owner cannot serve a screen message for supper. I want that last depot call treated as proper paid work.

headlineQuote: The restaurant owner cannot serve a screen message for supper.
portrait: Bianca is a **58-year-old** senior shortage-call agent with a two-year college diploma.
She earns **higher pay** and has eleven months of expenses saved.
She avoids **AI tools**, relying on signed load sheets and depot calls.
She compares **plentiful nearby suppliers** before leaving a paid lead row.
She will not assume **retirement income** or adult-child support.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when most shortage calls may vanish before a counter week appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Posted paid supplier rosters** with complete weekly wages, hours and handling duties.
